benchmark_type_evidence: we introduce AFROBENCH—a multi-task benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs across 64 African languages, 15 tasks and 22 datasets... Finally, we created a new evaluation dataset, AFRIADR, a dataset for restoring diacritic marks and tonal accents in African language texts.
brief_description: AfroBench is a comprehensive multi-task benchmark for evaluating LLM performance across 64 African languages, comprising 15 NLP tasks and 22 datasets spanning NLU, text generation, QA, and reasoning. It aggregates existing African language evaluation datasets and introduces one new dataset (AfriADR) for diacritics restoration.

all_annotators_native_speakers.evidence: Datasets from the Masakhane community likely involved native speakers. AfriADR was automatically generated. Translated datasets used professional translators whose nativeness is not confirmed.

annotator_workforce.evidence: AfroBench authors are from Masakhane NLP, Mila, McGill, Waterloo, UCL, The African Research Collective, and Lelapa AI. No ethics statement section is present. No annotator compensation or IRB details reported.

cultural_flags.english_centricity_notes: 9 of 22 datasets are translated from English. The benchmark uses English prompts for evaluation (cross-lingual prompting). Knowledge-intensive tasks (MMLU, Arc-Easy, MGSM) test Western-centric knowledge translated into African languages. However, the benchmark explicitly aims to address the underrepresentation of African languages in multilingual evaluations.

notably_excluded: Most of North Africa has only Arabic dialect representation
geographic_representation.evidence: Section 3.1: '64 African languages from seven language families (Afro-Asiatic, Atlantic-Congo, Austronesian, Indo-European, Mande, Nilotic, and English-Creole). 40 languages from Atlantic-Congo, 12 from Afro-Asiatic, 7 from Nilotic, 2 Indo-European, 2 Creole, 1 Austronesian.'

extraction_metadata.notes: AfroBench is primarily an aggregation benchmark (21 of 22 datasets are pre-existing), with one new dataset (AfriADR) created by the authors. The paper claims 64 languages but the detailed table lists approximately 65 distinct language entries including Luo appearing in both Nilotic and Niger-Congo sections. Language counts per dataset in the paper text occasionally differ from the data table.
